entries.title: Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican announces after surgery
entries.summary: Pope Leo XIV had surgery on Tuesday to remove a cancerous growth in his lung, the Vatican announced.
entries.content:
Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican announces after surgery

Pope Leo XIV had surgery on Tuesday to remove a cancerous growth in his lung, the Vatican announced.

The surgery, performed at Gemelli Hospital in Rome, involved removing the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung, according to a statement by Leo's doctors released by the church. Lung tissue examined after the surgery confirmed a previous test that revealed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said.

Adenocarcinoma of the lung is the most common form of lung cancer in the United States, representing about 40% of all lung cancers, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America.

The Pope's surgery, which the doctors said was successful, lasted about 90 minutes, after which Leo awoke normally and, following a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the hospital's 10th floor.

At 71 years old, Leo is relatively young for a pope – and remains physically active. He works out weekly, including regular tennis matches with his personal secretary and enjoys riding horses at Castel Gandolfo, the papal retreat.

Leo has not been known to smoke, but there is a history of cancer in the pope's family. On Tuesday, the Vatican announced that Leo's older brother Louis, who lives in Florida, is currently hospitalized with a form of cancer. And Leo's mother, Mildred, died of cancer in 1990 at age 77. Back in 1984, while living in Rome, the future pope wrote to several friends saying, "my mother continues to undergo chemotherapy treatments. … She's a tough lady and handles it all well, which makes it a little easier for me being so far from Chicago."

The Vatican says the Pope has essentially cleared his public schedule for the next several days, until at least October 20. The Vatican has yet to announce any further treatments.

entries.title: What an economics Nobel Prize winner knows about pricing
entries.summary: NPR's Ailsa Chang chats with Michael Woodford of Columbia University, who was one of two Americans awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics.
entries.content:
What an economics Nobel Prize winner knows about pricing

NPR's Ailsa Chang chats with Michael Woodford of Columbia University, who was one of two Americans awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics.

AILSA CHANG, HOST:

All right. Two Americans have just been awarded the Nobel Prize in economics. Robert Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University are being honored for their work on how to bring stability to cycles of economic boom and bust. But they base their macroeconomic models off of their microeconomic research into how people actually decide to buy stuff and how businesses actually decide to price that stuff. Economist Michael Woodford is with us now. Welcome, and congratulations on winning the Nobel Prize. I don't get to say that every day on the show (laughter) .

MICHAEL WOODFORD: (Laughter) I don't get to hear it every day, either. Thanks a lot.

CHANG: So what were your first thoughts when you found out you got the Nobel Prize?

WOODFORD: Well, I wasn't terribly awake, I'm afraid (laughter). I was trying to sleep when they called.

CHANG: Of course.

WOODFORD: Yeah. Because it's six hours later in Stockholm.

CHANG: Yeah. From the East Coast. Yeah.

WOODFORD: And my wife said I didn't sound very enthusiastic about it...

CHANG: (Laughter).

WOODFORD: ...But I mean, it was because I was...

CHANG: Groggy.

WOODFORD: ...At best, half awake.

(LAUGHTER)

CHANG: Well, I want to better understand your work, and I'm going to try to keep up as best I can, at least on the basic concepts. So part of your research was on how businesses set prices, right? And I want to use a very concrete example. Like, let's say you're a trucking company, and you're thinking about adjusting your rates because the cost of diesel fuel unexpectedly surges. How would your work apply to that example?

WOODFORD: Well, a thing that is particularly central to my work is stressing the extent to which decisions that people make often are forward-looking, are not just a response to immediate conditions...

CHANG: Yeah.

WOODFORD: ...But have to also take into account where you think things are headed. In the case of changes in costs that people have some reason to think is probably very temporary, I think, often, prices don't respond, that something that you think is likely to be lasting is going to be more likely to encourage people, more quickly, to already price it into the prices they're charging. So this issue of the extent to which people are able to make good guesses about where things are headed is something that the work that I've done particularly stresses.

CHANG: OK. Let me give you another concrete example.

WOODFORD: Sure.

CHANG: So, like, yesterday, the president of the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank said that she heard from a business owner who's planning to raise prices more than his costs have gone up because he just expects those costs to keep climbing. How concerning is that, when businesses start to anticipate higher costs and raise their own prices in response maybe disproportionately?

WOODFORD: Well, I think that illustrates that it isn't just the current costs...

CHANG: Yeah.

WOODFORD: ...That are going to matter for that decision. It matters a lot what people think about where they could be going, you know, their guesses, their fears. And that's one reason why my work has stressed the idea that policymakers should be concerned about trying to give people reassurances about, you know - not false reassurances - but if they themselves intend not to let certain things happen or to make them not very likely to happen, that being able to communicate that to the public so that their expectations about where things can go are, in fact, not significantly out of line with what really happened, that actually is important for the economy.

CHANG: If I could just jump in 'cause you're talking...

WOODFORD: Yeah.

CHANG: ...About something very important. You have stressed in your work that policymakers should make an effort to communicate clearly and accurately and in...

WOODFORD: Right.

CHANG: ...Proportion so that families and businesses can plan accordingly. How do you think Congress or President Trump or the Federal Reserve are doing on that front, on their communication skills? What do you think?

WOODFORD: Well, of course, it's a challenging thing. You know, I don't...

CHANG: (Laughter).

WOODFORD: ...Want to imply that I could just communicate much better than them. And, you know - but often policymakers don't think as much as they should about how important this is to their role. I think that, often, they take the view that it's enough to react to whatever is happening once it happens. You should think about the fact that your behavior being predictable actually has big benefits for the economy, and that people can see that this fits into a pattern of behavior that they can count on.

CHANG: So in this time where people are quite focused on affordability, what advice do you have for people out there feeling just unsettled and unsure about the state of the economy right now? Any words of assurance or warning (laughter)?

WOODFORD: Well, I certainly understand why it's an issue. I mean, it's not that economists should tell people to calm down. I think that it's appropriate for the government to indicate that it's keeping its eye on this issue, and to use monetary policy - make it clear that there is a commitment to keeping an eye on prices. I think it is - to some extent, it's a failure of public policy to not have kept a better lid on things.

CHANG: Michael Woodford, cowinner of the Nobel Prize in economics. Thank you, and congratulations again, Professor Woodford.

WOODFORD: Thanks.

entries.title: Bipartisan group of senators call on Trump to rescind Russian diesel deal
entries.summary: Six Democratic and six Republican senators wrote a letter calling on President Trump to withdraw from his recent deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
entries.content:
Bipartisan group of senators call on Trump to rescind Russian diesel deal

A bipartisan group of senators is calling on President Trump to rescind his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, calling it a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine."

Last week, Trump announced via social media he had struck a deal with Putin, whereby Russia will supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons "immediately thereafter."

"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Trump wrote.

His announcement stunned lawmakers, who passed legislation this summer directing the president to impose significant tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil.

Those sanctions are aimed at targeting Russian officials, companies and financial institutions helping fuel Russia's war in Ukraine. The legislation was named in memory of the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham, who helped negotiate Trump's support for the package.

"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies; it should be rescinded," wrote six Republican and six Democratic senators in a letter Tuesday to the president.

"The deal you struck with President Vladimir Putin on October 9th will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," it read.

Senators said they recognized the need to lower energy costs for Americans — but maintained that allowing Russian diesel into global markets will offer "limited to no relief to Americans."

They added the deal "only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians."

When asked about the letter, the White House referred back to comments President Trump made to reporters on Tuesday about concerns that Russia will use proceeds from the diesel agreement to purchase weapons.

"Nobody's telling me anything," Trump said. "That's a diesel deal. Not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us. That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market, because the world market suffered with high prices."

The letter was signed by Democrats Richard Blumenthal, Chris Coons, Dick Durbin, Jack Reed, Jeanne Shaheen and Sheldon Whitehouse. They were joined by Republicans Alan Armstrong, Susan Collins, John Cornyn, Mitch McConnell, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis.

entries.title: A judge blocks the government's tree-clearing spree at a municipal D.C. golf course
entries.summary: Locals and preservationists have long opposed Trump's plan to redevelop a municipal D.C. golf course. That legal fight escalated after the government cleared hundreds of trees on short notice.
entries.content:
A judge blocks the government's tree-clearing spree at a municipal D.C. golf course

A federal judge has temporarily barred the Trump administration from cutting down additional trees at a D.C. municipal golf course, the latest example of a court intervening in the government's efforts to reshape pieces of the nation's capital.

The long-simmering fight over East Potomac Golf Links — which President Trump wants to redevelop into a championship-level course — erupted over the weekend, after the administration cut down hundreds of trees with little notice.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes had ordered the administration in May to get court approval before cutting down more than 10 trees at the golf course. Officials notified the court just before 5 p.m. on Friday of their plan to remove "up to 529 trees" in phases starting on Saturday — and had razed at least 430 by the end of the day, prompting Reyes to call an emergency hearing on Monday.

"What has happened has cost the government all of its credibility with me in this case," Reyes said during the nearly four-hour hearing, held via videoconference.

Reyes ordered a short-term stop to the tree-clearings, which she extended on Tuesday through Oct. 26. She warned Monday that "if that order is violated by two seconds, there are going to be contempt proceedings."

Reyes also ordered top officials from the Department of Interior and the National Park Service to testify at a hearing next Monday, to shed more light on the government's motivations and the future of the historic course.

"The questions go to whether or not I've been lied to," Reyes said. "Whether I've been lied to in declarations about the plans, whether or not I've been lied to about the timing of things, and whether I've been lied to about what kind of notice the court was going to receive."

East Potomac has emerged as another flashpoint in Trump's unilateral quest to remake D.C., and it's the subject of a lawsuit by critics who fear it could go the way of the now-lost White House East Wing unless a court intervenes. The D.C. Preservation League, along with two concerned residents, sued the government in February over what it calls an unlawful takeover.

"This is a tactic we're seen before from the Trump-Vance administration – act quickly to irrevocably alter a cherished national landmark, just to advance another one of President Trump's pet vanity projects," Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward — one of the firms involved in the lawsuit — said in a statement this weekend.

Perryman told NPR on Tuesday that the golf course is the latest in a pattern of the Trump administration "undermining the entire checks and balances process in this country, which includes undermining court proceedings."

Trump has long floated the idea of redeveloping East Potomac into a championship-caliber course and announced plans to do so earlier this year, though his target Sept. 1 start date has come and gone without a formal proposal.

The prospect — and the lack of clarity since — has raised alarm among locals concerned about losing access to the historically affordable course and to the surrounding recreational area, which is popular with cyclists, runners, fishers and picnickers.

Loading...

"This is a broader story than just about golf, especially when there's been this little transparency, … to say, 'Here's what the future of this little man-made peninsula is actually going to look like,'" Alex Rosen, a D.C.-based consultant who started the nonprofit Save East Po, told NPR in July.

A National Park Service official said in a Friday court filing that plans for renovations "remain in the conceptual stage." And the Interior Department told NPR in a statement on Tuesday that it is "committed to continuing the relationships we have built with the local golf communities to ensure these courses are safe, beautiful, open, affordable, enjoyable, accessible, and world-class."

But critics are growing increasingly concerned about the process itself. They worry the Trump administration is using so-called routine maintenance as a pretext to begin redevelopment without the proper authorization.

"You can't continuously say, 'There's no plan' … while you're clearly taking steps to effect a plan," Rosen, who is not involved in the lawsuit, told NPR after watching the hearing. "It's just frankly lying."

Why the rush? The court hopes for answers next week

At Monday's hearing, Reyes expressed regret that she hadn't issued a formal restraining order earlier, which she said was because "I have done everything humanly possible to give the government the benefit of the doubt in this case."

For example, after the administration quietly removed what it has since said were roughly 150 dying and invasive trees in late August, Reyes acknowledged that people were upset but declined to intervene: "I am not the Lorax," she said at an early September hearing.

By Monday, that benefit of the doubt was gone. When a government lawyer said they had done their best to notify the court, Reyes offered a sharp rebuke.

"You did not do your best," she said, voice raised. "You did your absolute worst."

Perryman, of Democracy Forward, said, "What was really remarkable about the hearing yesterday is that the government did not appear to have a defense for its failure to notify the court."

In Friday's court filing, National Mall and Memorial Parks Superintendent Kevin Griess described the tree-clearing as part of an effort "to address deferred maintenance needs and implement treatment recommendations to restore the cultural landscape."

Griess specifically cited a 2019 National Park Service report about D.C. municipal golf courses, which says several waves of tree planting at East Potomac over the last century have obscured views and changed the feel of the course from its original 1920s "links-style" design.

Griess said in his filing that NPS was able to act on the report because it had received a temporary surge of "approximately 20 to 50 trained personnel capable of performing labor-intensive grounds maintenance activities." Under questioning in court, he confirmed that surge was connected to the administration's 250th anniversary events, including the IndyCar race on the National Mall in August.

But critics are skeptical, given the president's public statements. Alex Dickson, one of the plaintiffs, said in a statement that "the administration is using a preservation report as cover to begin tearing out the course it was written to save."

Griess said he had gotten the green light last week from Frank Lands, the park service's deputy director of operations. At the judge's request, Lands then joined the hearing from his car in a parking lot. He said he had gotten the directive from Greg Wischer, deputy chief of staff to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.

Wischer was not reachable to join the hearing, despite Reyes' request that he do so. She has ordered Wischer and Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, to testify at another hearing next Monday.

The Interior Department didn't answer NPR's questions about the timeline and resources for the tree-clearing, but said in a statement that "President Donald J. Trump is fulfilling his commitment to make D.C. Safe and Beautiful as shown by the working fountains, clean parks and safe streets across the district for the first time in decades."

In granting the plaintiffs' request for an extended restraining order on Tuesday, Reyes wrote that they had "proven they will likely suffer irreparable harm absent injunctive relief." She also said the government must provide "three business days' written advance notice prior to making any irreparable modification" to the golf course.

entries.title: Cornell University bans frat parties, vows to address 'disturbing' campus culture
entries.summary: In a letter, Cornell's president apologized for what happened to the student who alleges she was raped by several men at a fraternity house in 2024 and promised 'meaningful action.'
entries.content:
Cornell University bans frat parties, vows to address 'disturbing' campus culture

Cornell bans fraternity events for the rest of the school year

Cornell University has banned parties and social events at fraternities for the rest of the school year and will bring sexual assault investigators into its police unit, in response to a former student's allegation of gang rape in 2024.

The changes came on Tuesday as the university said it is committed to addressing a "deeply disturbing" culture of drug and alcohol abuse, and a rise in sexual violence on campus following a civil lawsuit filed by a former student, Jane Doe, which set off national outrage and a crisis at Cornell.

"I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," Michael I. Kotlikoff, who is Cornell's president, wrote in a letter addressed to the campus on Tuesday. "It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action."

The lawsuit, which Doe filed nearly one month ago, alleges that Doe was plied with ketamine and was sexually assaulted by members of the Chi Phi fraternity during a party in October of 2024. The details of the allegations, which disclosed how fraternity members used a Snapchat group chat to discuss the woman and events at the party with openly crude language, sparked fury across the nation.

Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told news outlets that Doe has been sent death threats and police swarmed her family's home since she filed the lawsuit.

The administration's changes come after student groups organized protests last week on campus.

"The administration is clearly feeling the heat and needed to make a move," says John Hartnett, a sophomore at Cornell who has helped organize protests. He called the changes a "half measure," and said that banning frats was not a long term solution to systematic issues at the university.

The faculty senate is considering a vote of no confidence in the university administration at a meeting scheduled for Wednesday. It's a rare move that demonstrates the deep seated frustration and distrust stemming from the 2024 case.

"Trust is still eroded on campus — that hasn't changed," says Julia Chang, an associate professor of Hispanic studies in the Department of Romance Studies. "The fact that these changes are coming about now — two years later — is a testament to the power of the student movement and the global conversation it has sparked; not the integrity of the administration."

The moratorium on events at fraternities is expected to have a reverberating effect on campus, where about one-third of all students participate in fraternities and sororities. The university's ties to Greek life, Kotlikoff said, has in part created a toxic culture on campus that requires serious course correction.

"While this is not a problem unique to Cornell, we are committed to setting a higher standard for education, oversight, and enforcement of safe social behavior and citizenship," Kotlikoff wrote.

Ray Epstein, who works with a consent education company, and is one of the organizers of a rally planned just steps away from Cornell's campus on Tuesday, said that while the measures from Cornell are "overall a win," they also serve as an "effort to save face."

"What I think they should be doing, is operating first instead of as a business, the way that they are now, as institutions that are meant to educate and keep their students safe," Epstein said.

Kotlikoff said that in addition to enhancing bystander training programming, the university will also improve its services to survivors of sexual assault by increasing staffing in its civil rights office, which would help individuals navigate the reporting process for incidents.

Additionally, the university will work with the New York State Police's criminal investigators on campus sexual assault investigations. The move allows the investigators, who are independent from the university, to take on cases in which survivors pursue criminal charges.

The university plans to bring in faculty who are experts in sexual assault and rape culture to help reform the Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault through listening events with the Cornell community.

Kotlikoff's letter did not explain why these events are only being issued now — two years after administrators at Cornell learned about the allegations in 2024.

Although the district attorney did not prosecute the case in 2024, Cornell's Title IX office conducted an investigation in 2025. In March 2025, a panel of staff and faculty at Cornell moved to expel or suspend some of the men. The panel required the remaining men to write "essays" in addition to other sanctions.

Cornell also barred the Chi Phi fraternity chapter, which was closed in 2024.

entries.title: The Trump administration warns Ukraine it could cut off intel, Zelenskyy tells NPR
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sat down for an interview with NPR at a time of renewed tensions with the White House.
entries.content:
KYIV, Ukraine — The Trump administration warned it could cut off intelligence-sharing with Ukraine unless Ukrainian forces stop long-range drone strikes on oil refineries inside Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told NPR.

In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, Zelenskyy said the Trump administration's decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel will not bring down fuel prices. He also refuted President Trump's assertion this weekend that Ukraine was to blame for the rise in diesel fuel prices. Zelenskyy pointed out it is because of the Iran war.

"Mostly people in the world know why their prices on any kind of energy, including diesel, raised up, why they increased. Because of Hormuz. Yes. Because of blocking the Strait of Hormuz," Zelenskyy said, referring to the vital shipping chokepoint between the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman.

President Zelenskyy's sit-down with NPR comes as Russia's full-scale invasion nears the five-year mark, at a time when the White House has renewed efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war. Tensions between Zelenskyy and President Trump have also flared up again after the U.S. made a key concession to Moscow.

On Friday, Trump moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Zelenskyy said in a statement it was a "a weak decision by strong partners."

Trump lashed back hard at Zelenskyy, saying, "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," a leader who can reach a peace deal with Putin.

Then on Sunday, Trump announced on social media Russia and Ukraine had allegedly agreed to a partial ceasefire to halt attacks on each other's energy infrastructure — catching Kyiv by surprise — even as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued.

Zelenskyy told NPR he found out about Trump's assertion of an energy ceasefire agreement "through social like you" — meaning, from Trump's post on his Truth Social account.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked Sunday about the announced energy truce and told reporters that contacts were ongoing.

Zelenskyy told NPR his country is striking Russian energy and logistics sites to weaken the Kremlin's ability to wage war. Ukraine wants the war to end, he said, but will not stop these strikes unless Russia stops attacking Ukrainian energy sites.

Putin doesn't respond to diplomacy, the Ukrainian leader said, "he understands force."

Meanwhile, high fuel prices have been a major concern in the U.S. as the midterm elections approach next month. In the U.S., diesel fuel costs an average of $6.27 per gallon — more than 70% above what it was a year ago when it was a little over $3.65 a gallon, according to AAA.

Zelenskyy said said Trump's decisions to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel would not influence "the price in the United States. I'm sure … because the volume is not enough."

What it would do, he said, is provide the Kremlin with more money to spend on its war.

Last year, the Trump administration paused intelligence-sharing with Ukraine amid tensions with Zelenskyy. The White House did not comment on whether the administration has threatened to do so again, instead referring NPR to comments Trump made Tuesday. "We are helping them and we are sharing intel, we want the war to end. So, we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end," Trump told reporters.

Later, Zelenskyy described a new Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital. "A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners," he wrote on social media.

He said the target was a power plant, and added, "It is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing."

entries.title: Writer Yiyun Li lost both of her sons. When words fell short, she turned to music
entries.summary: Li won a Pulitzer for her memoir about the suicides of her two sons. In her new novel, Music Against the Night, she writes about two young prodigies in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
entries.content:
Writer Yiyun Li lost both of her sons. When words fell short, she turned to music

If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

Writer Yiyun Li does not talk about "grief" or the "grieving process." To her, those words make it sound that at some point you emerge from grief. Instead, Li prefers to use the word "abyss," which, she says, is where she expects to be for the remainder of her life.

Li's teenage sons both died by suicide six years apart, Vincent in 2017 at age 16, and James in 2024 at age 19. Her Pulitzer Prize-winning 2025 memoir, Things in Nature Merely Grow, chronicled the loss of her sons and her effort to go on.

"James' death taught me to suffer better," she says. "To say, 'I can do it, and I can live with my pain and sorrow without ever wanting to stop feeling.'"

Li's new novel, Music Against the Night, is set in the late 1700s and early 1800s and centers on two prodigies who are brought together by music, and drawn apart because of their aspirations. The novel focuses on music, which sits outside of words.

"I think I've had the feeling both times after my children's death that words often fall short, and falling short doesn't mean not succeeding, falling short doesn't mean failing," she says. "But when I start a new project, I would like a subject [where] words naturally fall short. So music is that choice."

Li grew up in China and served a year in the Chinese military before coming to the U.S. to study immunology. She eventually left her Ph.D. program to become a writer. Li is now a professor in the creative writing program at Princeton University.

Interview highlights

On the decision to set Music Against the Night in a different time period

I was in the middle of the novel when James died. This is a novel far from my usual interests or concerns, and the reason I think I went back to history is I would like to live again through history, through historical figures, through my characters living in the late 18th and early 19th century. ... I'm making the past into a new now for myself and possibly for my readers.

On how playing piano connects to her grief

I began my piano lessons at the end of 2023, purely to get to know how to play the piano. And James died in February 2024, so two months into my piano lessons he died, and it occurred to me that piano or music is a good way for me to count time — because music is about time. It's about counting the measure, counting the rhythm. And also music is about ... be[ing] engaged with something else. You can sit in your sadness all day long, do nothing, or crying. Or, like me, I could just sit there and just play the same drill again, and again, as a way to know I was, in a way, staying in touch with the world. ...

I'm not a concert pianist, but somehow I find it liberating and healthy to do something that you absolutely love but cannot do well. Every time I go to my piano lesson, I'm so intimidated. I'm sweating because I just can't do it. I can hear other people do it, I cannot do it myself. But I think that's, again, acknowledging the limit of my capacity.

On raising two gifted children

Both my children could be called prodigies, but James, my younger son, especially was extraordinarily odd and brilliant. ... We were greatly baffled. I remember he was 5 or 6, he said, "Mommy, you will never see the world. I see it full of dots and squiggly lines." And that again was a strange perception of the world [that] we adults did not have access to. …

What is the responsibility or the difficulty of bringing up a child [who is] very brilliant? … Some people would say, well, you really have to train him to be the next Einstein, but we did not want him to be the next Einstein, we want him to be a normal, happy boy living in an ordinary life.

On her son Vincent

He was a brilliant painter and we still have all his paintings around the house. He was an oboist and when he wanted to learn the oboe, the oboe teacher said he was a bit young, because he was 8 when he want to learn oboe, but he was certain. ... [He had] started on the piano and he could articulate that piano was not his instrument. He wanted to play the oboe. But mostly, he wrote beautiful poetry. He was a great poet. And he was a greater reader. I wouldn't call him an outlier, as James was, but he was brilliant and fun and interesting.

On struggling with suicidal ideation

Sometimes I think people have all sort of thoughts about or against people who have chosen suicide, and people who've chosen or attempted suicide are often called selfish. But my experience is oftentimes people [are] in great pain, whether it's great mental pain or great physical pain. And sometimes people in deep depression cannot tell the difference between mental pain and physical pain, because everything together is a great kind of suffering. I think it's not that people who experience that kind of suicidal urge, it's not that they want to die or they want [to] use this to hurt other people.

On becoming a writer

I was born with innate curiosity and also sensitivity to things that did not quite make sense. So I grew up in China. And for instance, when I was little, all the adults would say, since you're a child, you have no right to decide who you want to be or what you want to do. And my mother even had a saying, something along the [lines] that an adult decides and the child follows. I was quite young, you know, 4 or 5. I just couldn't make sense of all of these teachings because I thought I was as capable of thinking as the adults, and why did I have to follow them? So I think that sort of sensitivity to things that are very, very nonsensical, I think maybe that's one thing that made me into a writer.

Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez Wisler produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

entries.title: Government spent millions on Trump ads. And, federal agents raid Ilhan Omar's home
entries.summary: The government is using millions of taxpayers' dollars on pro-Trump ads, even after the president said this would not happen. And, federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar's D.C. home.
entries.content:
Trump Midterm Campaigning, Rep. Omar Home Searched, Europe Pushes Back on Russia Deal

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The U.S. government continues to pay for ads promoting President Trump, even after he announced that his MAGA Inc. super PAC would take over funding. A federal judge ordered the ads to be taken down, yet they remained on air. An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer funds have been spent since the campaign began in late September. Almost $10 million of that was spent after Trump pledged on an Oct. 5 Truth Social post to fund the campaign privately. The White House has called the ads public service announcements, but a lawsuit by Common Cause and others argued they were funded without congressional approval, violating restrictions on taxpayer-funded publicity and propaganda.

Trump has ramped up his campaign travel ahead of the midterm elections. He rallied supporters in Youngstown, Ohio, last night and is heading to Alaska today. More events are planned for later this week. He has been trying to encourage his supporters to vote by telling them to pretend he is on the ballot.

  • 🎧 Trump's events resemble his presidential campaign rallies: He emphasizes his accomplishments while calling out superfans and insulting Democrats, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben tells Up First. Kurtzleben adds that Trump's campaign trail emphasizes that the GOP is still his party, despite his declining approval. Candidates like Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and GOP Sen. Jon Husted saw large, appreciative, but Kurtzleben says the benefits of appearing alongside Trump remain unclear.
  • ➡️ With just weeks until Election Day, polls may start to flood the landscape. While they serve as a helpful tool, remember they can't predict the future. Keep these tips in mind as polls pour in.
  • ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in Washington, D.C., yesterday morning. Omar, D-Minn., says the search was politically motivated by the Trump administration. The Department of Justice told NPR in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant," approved by the DOJ, as part of an ongoing federal investigation. Current and former federal officials with knowledge of the search who were not authorized to speak publicly confirmed the details, revealing that this multi-year probe includes whistleblower complaints and focuses on allegations of immigration fraud.

  • 🎧 One of Omar's neighbors, 79-year-old Sharon Jackson, tells NPR's Luke Garrett she was awoken yesterday at around 4:30 a.m. by loud knocking and that vans and agents wearing gloves were walking to and from the congresswoman's house. Vice President JD Vance previously accused Omar of immigration fraud, which she denies. Omar is an American citizen who left Somalia as a refugee. She stated on social media that the president has spent a decade targeting her with smear campaigns and vowed not to be silenced. Trump says that he is not involved in the investigation into Omar.

Living better

Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

The U.S. is experiencing its worst measles resurgence in decades. More than 3,600 confirmed cases and two deaths have been reported as of late September. Outbreaks in several states and exposures in public places like bars, sports stadiums and public transit have raised concerns about travel safety. Almost all U.S. measles cases involve unvaccinated individuals, and as the outbreaks grow in some states, the risk of exposure is getting higher. Here's what to know before traveling by plane or train.

  • ✈️ People who've had two doses of the MMR vaccine are considered protected against measles.
  • ✈️ The disease is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, breathes or sneezes. That airspace can remain contaminated for up to two hours.
  • ✈️ Check with your healthcare provider about your vaccination status. They may recommend a booster based on your medical history and health.
  • ✈️ Immunocompromised individuals may be unable to receive vaccination and often rely on herd immunity for protection. For measles, the vaccination threshold for herd immunity is 95%.
  • ✈️ Measles can be hard to track because symptoms — such as fever, cough, and rash — typically appear seven to 14 days after exposure and can sometimes take long as 21 days to surface.

Picture show

The Metropolitan Museum of Art's new blockbuster exhibition showcases the works of two 20th-century artists. Jackson Pollock is well-known for his drip paintings. His wife, Lee Krasner, has often been overshadowed by her husband. This show finally gives Krasner the recognition she deserves. With more than 120 pieces on display — 74 from Krasner and 48 from Pollock — the show highlights Krasner as a titan of Abstract Expressionism, too. Check out some of the photos from the exhibit.

3 things to know before you go

  • Americans Robert Hall from Stanford University and Michael Woodford from Columbia University have won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on managing boom-and-bust cycles to reduce inflation and unemployment.
  • Trump's new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, will hold her first press briefing today. She has raised her profile by appearing on conservative outlets and promoting right-wing conspiracy theories.
  • Hectic early-morning traffic can make breakfast a luxury in Lagos, Nigeria. Akara is a roadside staple. For NPR's Breakfast Around the World series, Emmanuel Akinwotu explores the savory snack's deep roots in Nigeria and West Africa, and its spread around the world during the trans-Atlantic slave trade.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

entries.title: What ice cream has to do with this year's Nobel Prize in economics
entries.summary: Prices can get sticky. That helps explain why recessions hurt so much — and what policymakers can do about them.
entries.content:
What ice cream has to do with this year's Nobel Prize in economics

This article first appeared in the Planet Money newsletter. You can sign up here.

On Monday morning, the world's econ nerds tuned in to an announcement from Sweden to learn who won this year's Nobel Prize in economics. And we got a lesson involving … ice cream.

The winners were Robert Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University. The prize committee honored them "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization."

To explain what the heck that means — as we will try to do in this newsletter — Timo Boppart, an economist at Stockholm University and member of the prize committee, stood up and walked around like he was giving a TED Talk. At one point, he brought up an image on the screen behind him: an ice cream menu.

Boppart used the ice cream menu to serve up a sweet lesson in economics.

"How do firms actually set prices?" Boppart asked. " This is illustrated here with this ice cream menu. Prices do not adjust [on] a continuous basis. Firms instead set the price of this ice cream for a whole season."

Ice cream was a poetic example. Because prices, like ice cream, can get sticky. In fact, economists use the term "sticky prices" to describe how prices can stubbornly stay put even as economic conditions change.

That seemingly minor detail can have huge consequences for the entire economy. Sticky prices are a cornerstone of what's known as "New Keynesian economics" — a framework that has helped reshape macroeconomic theory and how policymakers think about fighting recessions and controlling inflation.

This year's prize honored work that helped lay the foundations for New Keynesian economics. In the process, Hall, Woodford, and other scholars helped breathe new life into the ideas of economics giant John Maynard Keynes, whose intellectual legacy, for a time, seemed in danger of melting away.

To understand why, we need to go back to the 1970s, when the economy experienced something that, for some, seemed to invalidate Keynesian economics.

Keynesianism gets a brain freeze

John Maynard Keynes is basically the father of macroeconomics, the study of how the entire economy works, including what the government can do to fight recessions, boost employment, and control inflation.

Keynes' breakthrough came in the depths of the Great Depression, when he published The General Theory of Employment, Interest, and Money. He articulated an idea that may seem obvious today but challenged the economic orthodoxy of his time: an economy can get stuck in a prolonged slump, and the free market won't necessarily get everyone back to work on its own. Instead, Keynes wrote, we needed the government to help boost spending, put people back to work, and return the economy to health.

If you've ever taken an Econ 101 class, you've probably heard about the "invisible hand" of the free market. It's the idea that people and businesses pursuing their own interests in competitive markets can help the economy reach its full potential without the government having to step in. Keynes basically argued we couldn't count on the invisible hand to pull the economy out of a slump. We needed the visible hand of the government.

Keynes influenced an entire generation of economists and policymakers. Even Milton Friedman, a strong advocate for the free market, was quoted in 1965 as saying, "We are all Keynesians now." (He later said the quote was taken out of context.)

In the 1970s, however, the dominant Keynesian models — and the policies they helped guide — ran into trouble. Inflation and unemployment rose together — a painful combination known as "stagflation." The existing Keynesian models struggled to explain it.

"For a long time, the recipes of Keynes seemed to work, but they then failed during the oil crisis in the 1970s when high unemployment and high inflation took over simultaneously," said John Hassler, the chair of the Nobel committee, when they announced the prize.

When the old-school models faltered, some economists wanted to reject Keynes wholesale. Economists like Robert Lucas and Edward Prescott — who each won Nobel Prizes — challenged Keynesian economics and its confidence that government policy could effectively smooth out the economy's ups and downs. Call it the revenge of the invisible hand.

A central criticism: The Keynesian models relied too heavily on patterns found in past economic data without adequately explaining the individual decisions behind them. Addressing that criticism meant giving models "microfoundations": starting with the decisions of individual people and businesses to explain how the whole economy works. The economy is made of people, and people think ahead. They anticipate what policymakers will do, and those expectations shape how they spend, save, and invest. If policymakers change direction, people's behavior might too — making old patterns an unreliable guide to whether a new policy will work.

One influential alternative to Keynesianism, developed by Prescott and other economists, became known as "real business cycle" theory. These models assumed that prices and wages were completely flexible, adjusting freely as economic conditions changed. If demand for workers fell, wages could fall too, making workers cheaper to hire and allowing the labor market to balance supply and demand. That left little room for a familiar feature of recessions: people who want to work but can't find jobs.

Gregory Mankiw, now an economist at Harvard University, entered graduate school at MIT alongside Michael Woodford in 1980. They were learning macroeconomics just as economists were fighting over how to rebuild it.

"Lucas and Prescott were ascendant, but a lot of us were skeptical of their conclusions," Mankiw tells Planet Money. " And that's when people like Woodford and Hall sort of entered the stage. The sense was that the people who were rejecting the Keynesian model were throwing out the baby with the bathwater. And so rather than throwing it out, they wanted to sort of fix the problems."

A fresh scoop of Keynes

Hall and Woodford helped rebuild macroeconomics around the decisions of individual people and businesses. Hall broke new ground in understanding how people's expectations about the future shape their spending today. Woodford built on that work, developing a framework that combined forward-looking spending decisions with sticky prices.

To see why sticky prices matter, let's return to the ice cream example. Say there's a recession and demand for ice cream plummets. Shops might not quickly reduce ice cream prices to entice customers back. Maybe changing menus and signs costs time and money. Or maybe shops aren't yet sure whether the drop in demand is temporary or here to stay. Instead, they keep prices frozen, sell fewer scoops, and ultimately may end up having to cut worker hours or lay people off. When prices don't adjust, jobs and businesses take a hit.

The same story goes for wages, which we guess are a bigger factor in the economy than ice cream prices.

" When economists talk about sticky prices, they're also including sticky wages — the price of labor," Mankiw says. "Most people don't get their wages adjusted every month."

Across the economy, that stickiness or "price rigidity" can have big consequences. When spending drops, prices and wages don't quickly and flexibly adjust to keep people buying and businesses hiring. Instead of prices falling to bring supply and demand together, in these models, price stickiness causes production and employment to fall. It helps explain why, during recessions, people who want to work can remain out of a job for long stretches.

" Bringing in those price rigidities into the framework was absolutely key because this is the reason why the invisible hand cannot do its magic and there is room for policy intervention," said Boppart at the Nobel Prize announcement.

In other words, even when people and businesses think ahead and act in their own interests, sticky prices can keep the economy stuck in a slump. Call it Keynes' comeback. In these models, governments and central banks still have a role to play in getting the economy back on track.

This was the promise of New Keynesian economics: take the criticisms of the old models seriously, rebuild models around individual decisions, and preserve Keynes' central insight that the free market won't always bounce back on its own.

"One thing that clearly differentiates Keynesian models from Real Business Cycle models was the flexibility or stickiness of prices," Mankiw says. "Most economists today — not all — but I think most economists today buy into the sticky price assumption."

These New Keynesian models became integral to how governments and central banks think about fighting recessions and controlling inflation.

Woodford's work, for example, helped lay the theoretical groundwork for "forward guidance," a strategy the Federal Reserve used during the Great Recession. The Fed slashed its benchmark interest rate to near zero, but the economy still needed stimulus. So under then-chair Ben Bernanke, the Fed signaled that it expected to keep interest rates low for an extended period. By shaping expectations about future rates, the Fed tried to help lower longer-term borrowing costs and encourage spending today.

Keynes' ideas survived with new foundations. And Mankiw offers an update to Milton Friedman's famous line: "We're all New Keynesians now," he says.

P.S. Throughout this piece, we've called this award the "Nobel Prize in economics." But calling it that is surprisingly controversial. Technically, it has a much clunkier name. Economics wasn't one of the prizes Alfred Nobel created. So how did it join the club? Ricky and I tell that story in the latest episode of The Indicator from Planet Money. Check it out when it's released Tuesday.
